page: Microsoft Azure D48ls_v7 is a compute-oriented virtual machine belonging to the Dlsv7 server family. It is powered by an Intel Xeon 6973P-C processor with x86_64 architecture, operating at a clock speed of 4.2 GHz. The instance features 48 dedicated vCPUs derived from 24 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. It is equipped with 96.0 GB of system memory, yielding a low memory-to-core ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU. No local storage or GPUs are bundled with this instance, though it is Premium Storage capable.

Benchmark data reveals strong compute capabilities, particularly in instruction execution and compression. The single-threaded gzip compression reaches 36.1 GB/sec, and single-threaded bzip3 decompression achieves 15.17 GB/sec, both placing in the top tier. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression registers at 303.78 GB/sec, and the PassMark CPU score is 66066.16, both categorized as strong. In memory performance, the instance records a read-only small block cached bandwidth of 3532.24 GB/sec, while large block uncached read and write bandwidths are 173.98 GB/sec and 68.56 GB/sec, respectively.

The underlying Intel Xeon processor supports advanced instruction sets, including Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX-512) and Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) for integer and bfloat16 operations. These hardware features support tasks like low-latency LLM inference, where the server achieves 331.81 tokens/sec for text generation on a small 135M model and 27.47 tokens/sec on a medium 7B model. However, performance drops to an average tier of 2.92 tokens/sec for large 70B models due to memory constraints.

The primary tradeoff of the D48ls_v7 is its low memory density of 2.0 GB per vCPU, which limits its suitability for memory-intensive databases or massive datasets. However, the high clock speed and dedicated CPU allocation make it cost-efficient for compute-heavy workloads that do not require large memory footprints. Appropriate workloads include static web serving, which benchmarked at 75.36 GB/sec, Redis operations at 79.02 million operations per second, CPU-bound batch processing, and lightweight machine learning inference.
